messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Authority Presence: Police, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Maly Phommasack is a 51-year-old Lao-American physician, married and working as an internist at a busy urban outpatient clinic in the Pacific Northwest. She presented for psychological consultation approximately eight months after an assault that she described, haltingly and with visible effort, as the most disorienting experience of her life — not only because of what happened, but because of how completely it had dismantled everything she had quietly assumed to be true about the world she inhabited.

The assault occurred on a Tuesday evening in late autumn when Maly stayed after hours to complete charting. The clinic had emptied. A man she did not recognise forced his way into an exam room where she was working alone, and in the silence of the building — that particular quality of stillness that comes after the last receptionist leaves — he attacked her. The assault was prolonged and physically brutal. At one point he pinned her arm against the exam table with a force that left lasting soft-tissue injury, and she recalls the specific, close-range details of his hands and forearms with a clarity that has never faded. When it was over he left without a word. Maly lay on the floor for some time before calling for help. Police arrived within minutes, and she remembers sitting in a waiting-room chair, wrapped in an emergency blanket, watching two uniformed officers move through her clinic with clipboards and radios, feeling simultaneously grateful and, in a way she could not then articulate, profoundly unsafe.

In the weeks that followed, the assault did not recede the way Maly had expected it to. She had treated trauma patients herself; she understood, intellectually, that recovery was not linear. What she had not anticipated was the way her own memory refused to behave like memory. When something pulled her back to that evening — the particular smell of antiseptic that permeated every exam room in her clinic, a smell she had never before registered consciously — the terror did not arrive as recollection. It arrived as the thing itself, indistinguishable from the original. She had told her husband that trying to describe what happened felt impossible, that the memory was so extreme it was hard to believe it had actually happened to her at all, and yet her body treated it as perpetually present. The story felt simultaneously unreal and inescapable.

Maly returned to work after three weeks, which she now regards as both a professional necessity and a decision made without full understanding of what she was returning to. Her clinic required her to examine patients' hands, arms, and torsos dozens of times each day. The sight of a male patient's forearm on the exam table — something she had performed thousands of times across her career — could arrest her mid-sentence. She began scheduling her most physically demanding examinations early in the morning, reasoning that she was sharper then, though she understood privately that what she was managing was not fatigue. She started wearing long-sleeved shirts and high-necked blouses every day, even in summer, having come to feel that making herself less visible in some way reduced her exposure to a danger she could not fully name. She stopped taking the direct route past the police precinct on her commute. If an unexpected noise — a door slamming in the corridor, a dropped instrument tray — reached her while she was with a patient, she would feel her attention leave the room entirely, scanning for the source with an alertness that was exhausting to sustain.

She had not told her colleagues what was happening. She had not told most of her friends. She had begun driving to a casino on the far side of the city on Friday evenings, initially once a month, then most weeks, drawn by the noise and the crowds and the specific quality of absorption that slot machines produced — a state in which nothing from that Tuesday evening could find purchase. Her husband had noticed the absences. Their conversations had become careful and abbreviated.

What finally brought Maly to seek help was seeing the man who had assaulted her in a pharmacy three weeks before her intake appointment. He was standing in the checkout line. She left her basket on the floor and walked out without speaking to anyone, drove home, and sat in her car in the driveway for two hours. She had come to believe, in the months since the assault, that she could manage this alone — that thinking about it directly would undo her in some way she would not recover from, and that the world she had once trusted to be basically safe was simply gone, replaced by something she no longer knew how to navigate. What frightened her most, sitting in that intake room, was not the work of therapy itself but the possibility that the person she had been before that Tuesday evening was no longer retrievable.
